newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Thirteen firms to bid for Guatemala power plants.
newsitem.headline: Thirteen firms to bid for Guatemala power plants.

text.p: Thirteen companies from the United States, Europe and South America are competing to purchase two electric plants for $30 million as Guatemala privatizes electric production, bidding consultants said on Wednesday.

Interested companies paid $2,500 as a preliminary step in the bidding, and can still drop out of the process or join together in consortium, said Peter Macaulay, executive director of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

The companies are: AES Americas, of AES Corp. ; Calpine Corp ; Coastal Power; Constellation Power; Destec Energy ; Endesa; Enron Caribe, of Enron Corp.; International Energy Partners; Marathon Power; Max Power; Megatron Power Corp.; Perez Compac ; and Union Fenosa ACEX.
"Interest is keen because of what is happening to the industry in the United States," Macaulay said at a press conference. "They're looking for other places to make money."
The Guatemalan Electric Company (EEGSA) is selling the thermoelectric power plants, with a combined capacity of 80 megawatts, as part of the General Electricity Law passed by Congress in September.
The law ends the government monopoly on electricity production and allows new producers to sell electricity directly to consumers on the open market.

The winning bid will offer the lowest price per kilowatt hour and the greatest capacity, as the $30 million purchase price is set, Macaulay said. Bids are due on May 23 and a decision will be announced June 30.

The firms are bidding on a Power Purchase Agreement to buy 90 percent of the assets. The remaining 10 percent, valued at an additional $3 million, will be held in reserve through the end of the year to give employees the option of securing financing to purchase shares in the new company, said Julio Campos, president of the Electric Company.

The Electric Company sells power to residents of Guatemala City and the greater metropolitan area. It owes $85 million to the National Electrification Institute (INDE), which sells power to the national company and to consumers outside the metropolitan area.

The sale of the Laguna plant in Amatitlan, about 12 miles (20 km) from the capital, and the Stewart & Stevenson plant in the coastal province of Escuinta, is designed to reduce that debt and improve and expand service, Campos said.

Barely 47 percent of Guatemalans have access to electrical service, Campos said. Energy officials hope to serve 70 percent by 2000, and to increase capacity of the two plants to 150 megawatts within 18 years.
